source.title: Understanding quantum machine learning also requires rethinking generalization
source.authors: Elies Gil-Fuster; J. Eisert; Carlos Bravo-Prieto

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including supplementary material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs randomization experiments on quantum neural networks, extending the random-label memorization finding to quantum models and quantum data. Its results do not test the claim versions about standard deep networks trained on images.
record.gate_note: The empirical results test analogous behaviors in QCNNs. Because the claim versions specify standard deep networks and image inputs, no result is mapped to V1–V6. The paper also discusses prior classical results, which are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study tests analogous memorization phenomena in parameterized quantum circuits trained with CMA-ES, a derivative-free optimizer. These are fundamentally different systems from the standard deep networks in V1–V6, so its own results do not test any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors demonstrate QCNN memorization empirically and conditional quantum-circuit expressivity analytically. They argue that distribution-independent uniform generalization bounds are vacuous in the tested memorization regimes, without disproving the bounds or explaining successful generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study adapts randomization tests to quantum phase classification with QCNNs and quantum-state inputs. It changes the model and data domain from the cited classical deep-network image experiments; training uses CMA-ES, a stochastic derivative-free optimizer.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-set size affects the reported generalization gap; label-corruption fraction affects test error and optimization behavior. Random initialization is reported to affect when training error begins to decrease.

fits_no_version.finding: QCNNs fit random labels for small quantum-phase training sets, with a generalization gap near 0.75; fitting deteriorates as training-set size increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: QCNNs trained with CMA-ES can memorize random labels on small quantum-state datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: QCNNs achieve 100% training accuracy across corruption levels for N = 4, 6, 8, while test error rises toward 75%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: QCNNs can fit partially corrupted quantum-phase labels while retaining some predictive signal.

fits_no_version.finding: For N = 6, fully randomized labels converge slightly faster on average than real labels; intermediate corruption produces substantial variation in convergence onset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: QCNN optimization time need not increase monotonically with label corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: QCNNs perfectly fit small datasets of amplitude-randomized quantum states, with test performance no better than random guessing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: QCNNs can memorize labels on the study's randomized quantum-state inputs.

record.problems: The numerical evidence is limited to one architecture and one quantum-phase classification task. The random-label and random-state experiments use small training sets (up to 20). Figure 3 contains several condition-specific values without exact values in the text; the text reports trends and selected summaries.
record.rows_left_out: No result-bearing empirical outcomes on the claim's specified classical deep networks or image inputs are present. Theoretical constructions and cited results are not rows under the result-row criteria.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting by standard deep networks trained with stochastic gradient methods under unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time and corruption-dependent convergence in the specified deep networks.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs with the same deep networks.
Perfect training fit and steady test-error degradation across label corruption in the specified deep networks.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Whether deep networks learn shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels; aggregate QCNN learning curves do not distinguish these components.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T3 classification conflicts with its correct decision to link no rows to V1–V6. The exclusion rests on the quantum model and training procedure, not a blanket requirement for image data: V1 does not explicitly restrict the input domain to images. Row states here describe their inability to determine the listed versions; the quantum analogues themselves are observed.

versions.untested_parts: All parts: the study tests QCNNs on quantum states, not standard deep networks on training images.
All parts: training-time comparisons are for QCNNs on quantum data, not standard deep networks on images.
All parts: random quantum states are not shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise images.
All parts: the corruption sweep is in a QCNN quantum-phase task, not the specified deep networks and image task.
All parts: the study does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation in standard deep networks.
All parts: the paper does not test whether standard deep networks learn real-label patterns before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on quantum phase data with labels replaced by uniformly random labels; compared with real-label training.
rows.measure: Empirical generalization gap; training and test error/accuracy.
rows.baseline: Real-label training is shown as a comparison; exact baseline values not stated.
rows.value: For random labels, the gap is close to 0.75, described as effectively maximal; the text attributes this to perfect training accuracy and test accuracy equal to random guessing. The largest gap occurs with training set size up to N = 10; it diminishes as training set size increases.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 3(a) shading is standard deviation across experiment repetitions; exact values not stated.
rows.locator: Results, Numerical results, Random labels; Fig. 3(a)
rows.note: The figure averages the generalization gap across the different qubit numbers for each training-set size; it does not provide separate textual values by qubit number. This is a quantum-data result, not a result on images.
rows.check: The reported quantum result is accurate, but cannot establish a listed version. Perfect fitting is restricted to small training sets; training accuracy decreases as set size increases.

rows.subject: quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN)

rows.subject: quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN)
rows.operation_detail: Measured training error over training time while fitting corrupted quantum labels.
rows.measure: Training error during optimization; average convergence time.
rows.baseline: r = 0 (uncorrupted labels); exact convergence time not stated.
rows.value: Intermediate corruption levels show a long, stable plateau; the plateau has significant variance. For r = 1, the QCNN on average fits the training data slightly faster than for r = 0.
rows.uncertainty: Variance over five experiment repetitions with independently initialized QCNN parameters; exact values not stated.
rows.locator: Results, Numerical results, Corrupted labels; Fig. 3(b) inset
rows.note: No numeric time ratio is reported, and the stated comparison is for the QCNN quantum-data task.
rows.check: This measures QCNN optimization with CMA-ES, outside V2. Clarify that the intermediate-corruption plateau is an average of runs that have or have not converged, rather than a plateau within each run.

relation.reason: The study discusses classical randomization findings and their relationship to its quantum experiments, without testing a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The study tests analogous memorization in quantum circuits with quantum-state inputs and CMA-ES optimization. These systems do not meet the standard deep-network scope of V1–V6; the classical finding motivates the experiments rather than serving as a tool.

source_check.notes: R3's intermediate-corruption plateau is an average over converged and unconverged runs, not a sustained intermediate plateau within each run. R1 and R4 report perfect fitting for small training sets; the displayed pack truncates some row fields.
